facts.statement: Kepodactylus lived during the Late Jurassic period in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, United States.
facts.quote: Kepodactylus is an extinct genus of ctenochasmatid pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Kimmeridgian-Tithonian-age Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation of Colorado, United States.

facts.statement: Fossils of Kepodactylus were discovered in 1992 in Garden Park, Colorado, while a team excavated a Stegosaurus specimen.
facts.quote: In 1992, a team from the Denver Museum of Natural History dug up a specimen of the dinosaur Stegosaurus stenops in Garden Park, Colorado. In the quarry they also found smaller disarticulated bones from other animals, among which were those of a pterosaur new to science.

facts.statement: Jerald Harris and Kenneth Carpenter named the genus Kepodactylus and its type species K. insperatus in 1996.
facts.quote: In 1996, Jerald Harris and Kenneth Carpenter named the new genus. The type species is Kepodactylus insperatus.

facts.statement: The genus name Kepodactylus combines Greek words for "garden" and "finger" to reference its discovery site and pterosaur anatomy.
facts.quote: The genus name is derived from Greek, kepos, "garden", a reference to Garden Park and daktylos, "finger", referring to the typical wing finger of pterosaurs.

facts.statement: The species name insperatus means "unhoped-for" because the researchers originally hoped to find a dinosaur, not a pterosaur.
facts.quote: The specific name means "unhoped-for" in Latin, alluding to the fact that the researchers hoped to find a dinosaur, and did not expect a pterosaur.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen DMNH 21684 consists of a cervical vertebra, a left humerus, finger bones, and a metatarsal.
facts.quote: The species is based on the holotype DMNH 21684, consisting of a cervical vertebra, the left humerus, several finger bones, and a metatarsal.

facts.statement: Kepodactylus had a wingspan of about 2.5 meters and possessed additional pneumatic foramina in its vertebrae and humerus.
facts.quote: Kepodactylus was similar to Mesadactylus but with a larger wingspan of around 2.5 m [8.2 ft] and with additional pneumatic foramina (holes to allow air from air sacks to enter the bones) in the vertebrae and humerus.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the mass of Kepodactylus at approximately 10 kilograms (22 lbs) in 2022.
facts.quote: In 2022 Gregory S. Paul estimated its mass at 10 kg (~22 lbs).

facts.statement: David Unwin considered Kepodactylus to be a basal member of the Dsungaripteroidea.
facts.quote: Unwin lo consideró como un miembro basal de los Dsungaripteroidea sensu Unwin.

rejected.statement: Phylogenetic analysis by Longrich, Martill, and Andres in 2018 recovered Kepodactylus as a basal member of the family Ctenochasmatidae.
rejected.quote: They recovered Kepodactylus as a basal member of the family Ctenochasmatidae.

rejected.statement: The morphology of the proximal wing finger phalanx in Kepodactylus is most similar to that of Rhamphorhynchus.
rejected.quote: The proximal wing finger phalanx in Kepodactylus is most similar in morphology to that of Rhamphorhynchus.

rejected.statement: The metatarsal of Kepodactylus is morphologically very similar to the metatarsal of digit IV of the dimorphodontid pterosaur Dimorphodon.
rejected.quote: The metatarsal that was found of Kepodactylus is morphologically very similar to the metatarsal of digit IV of Dimorphodon, a dimorphodontid pterosaur.
